title: A temporary capital
text: Lieutenant-Governor John Graves Simcoe founds York as a "temporary" capital of Upper Canada while he plans a permanent one near today's London, Ontario. The townsite is ten compact blocks near the mouth of the Don River, with a garrison at the entrance to the harbour. In 1796 York becomes the permanent capital.

title: The Americans land
text: On April 27, 1813, an American force lands on the western lakeshore and captures York. The retreating British blow up the fort's powder magazine, killing the American commander, Brigadier General Zebulon Pike. The town is looted and burned. The fort is rebuilt between 1813 and 1815 and still stands.

title: York becomes Toronto
text: On March 6, 1834, the town is incorporated as the City of Toronto. The new name sets it apart from New York and from about a dozen other Yorks in the province. Immigration has taken it from 1,700 people in 1826 to 9,254.

title: The Cathedral Fire
text: On April 7, 1849, the city's first major fire wipes out much of the Market Block, the business core. The church that stood where St. James Cathedral is now burns with it. The cathedral on the site today was built afterwards.

title: The railway arrives
text: On May 16, 1853, the first train of the Ontario, Simcoe and Huron Railway runs from Toronto to Machell's Corners, today's Aurora. It is the first steam railway to enter service in what was then Upper Canada, and it reaches Collingwood on Georgian Bay in 1855.

title: Gooderham and Worts
text: The distillery founded in 1832 on the waterfront grows into one of the largest in Canada. Its buildings from the 1860s survive: more than forty of them, the largest collection of Victorian-era industrial architecture in North America. The site reopened in 2003 as the Distillery District.

title: Electric streetcars
text: On August 15, 1892, the Toronto Railway Company starts converting the horse-drawn streetcar system it took over the year before to electric trams. The company runs the city's streetcars until 1921.

title: A city hall ten years in the making
text: Edward James Lennox's city hall at Queen and Bay opens after more than a decade of construction and a bill of more than $2.5 million. It is the largest civic building in North America. Councillors, angry about the delays and the cost, refuse Lennox a plaque naming him as architect.

title: The Great Fire
text: On the evening of April 19, 1904, fire breaks out in a neckwear factory at 58 Wellington Street West, just west of Bay. It destroys more than a hundred buildings in the downtown core and kills one person.

title: A bridge with room for a subway
text: The Prince Edward Viaduct joins Bloor Street to Danforth Avenue across the Don Valley. Its designers add a lower deck for a rapid transit line that does not exist yet, a cost that is controversial at the time. The Bloor–Danforth subway starts using it in 1966.

title: Union Station
text: On August 6, 1927, Prince Edward, Prince of Wales, opens Union Station with a pair of gold scissors. In the Great Hall he remarks: "You build your train stations like we build our cathedrals."

title: Tallest in the British Empire
text: The Canadian Bank of Commerce opens its 34-storey limestone headquarters at King and Bay, now Commerce Court North. It stays the tallest building in the British Empire and Commonwealth until 1962.

title: Canada's first subway
text: On March 30, 1954, after five years of construction, the Yonge subway opens: 7.4 kilometres under Yonge Street from Union Station to Eglinton Avenue. It is Canada's first underground passenger rail line.

title: New City Hall
text: On September 13, 1965, Governor General Georges Vanier opens the new City Hall and Nathan Phillips Square. The design by Finnish architect Viljo Revell won an international competition in 1958, the first in Ontario open to architects from abroad.

title: Black towers on Bay Street
text: The Toronto-Dominion Bank Tower is finished: 222.8 metres, the tallest building in Canada. Ludwig Mies van der Rohe was design consultant for the complex of bronze-tinted glass and black steel. It stands on the block where the Great Fire of 1904 began.

title: The expressway that stopped
text: On June 3, 1971, Premier William Davis cancels the Spadina Expressway, partly built and headed for downtown, after public opposition. The decision ends the other expressways planned into and around the city. The subway line that was part of the plan is built anyway.

title: The CN Tower
text: The CN Tower opens on June 26, 1976, on railway lands that were being made redundant. At 553.3 metres it holds the record as the world's tallest free-standing structure for 32 years.

title: SkyDome
text: SkyDome opens beside the tower on June 3, 1989: the first stadium with a fully retractable motorized roof. It was renamed Rogers Centre in 2005.

title: The megacity
text: On January 1, 1998, the Ontario government dissolves Metropolitan Toronto and its six municipalities, East York, Etobicoke, North York, Scarborough, York and the old City of Toronto, and merges them into one city. This map covers the old city only.

title: Towers on the railway lands
text: Concord Adex bought the empty railway lands west of the SkyDome in 1997. The first four towers of CityPlace are finished in 2002 and 2003, and more follow through the decade.

title: What this map shows
text: Every building here is one that still stands today, so the early city looks emptier than it was. About one building in seven has a year from a record. The rest are estimates from the census and from dated neighbours. Click any building to see where its year comes from.
